slides.title: Bits give possibilities; a format gives meaning
keyPoints: Four bits provide 16 patterns
The same pattern can have different interpretations
The protocol decides which patterns are valid
slides.narration: Four independent positions with two choices each give sixteen possible patterns. That arithmetic does not tell us whether a pattern means a count, a permission set, or a reserved state. For example, 1010 is ten under an unsigned interpretation, but a format might use it as two separate flags and a small mode field. A debugger can display the same storage in binary, hexadecimal, or decimal without changing it. Begin a bit-level problem by naming the interpretation and numbering the positions. Only then can we judge whether a mask or shift performs the required operation. The representation is concrete; its application meaning is a separate contract.
actions: Write one four-bit pattern and propose two different legitimate interpretations.

question.prompt: Does having 16 four-bit patterns imply that all 16 are valid modes?
question.answer: No. A protocol can reserve patterns or restrict the semantic mode values.

slides.title: A numeral is a notation, not a sequence of digit bytes
keyPoints: 0x2D and decimal 45 denote the same value
One hex digit corresponds to four bits
The text 45 is a different representation
slides.narration: Hexadecimal 2D contains two times sixteen plus thirteen, giving forty-five. Its binary form is 0010 1101, since each hexadecimal digit maps to four bit positions. Writing that numeric literal in source does not mean memory stores the character codes for 2 and D. A text representation is a different object with an encoding and a length. This distinction matters in parsers and binary files: converting a displayed number back to a value is not the same operation as copying an integer's bytes. Choose binary when positions matter, hex when grouped patterns matter, and decimal when a human count is the clearest view.
actions: Convert 0x2D to binary and decimal, then contrast it with two text characters.

question.prompt: Do the numeric literal 45 and the string literal "45" have the same representation contract?
question.answer: No. One denotes an integer value; the other denotes character code units that a parser could interpret as a number.

slides.title: Some required bits is not all required bits
keyPoints: Bitwise AND keeps matching positions
Any tests for a nonzero intersection
All compares the intersection with the full mask
slides.narration: The required mask has bits three and two set, while flags has only bit two. Bitwise AND keeps that common bit, so any is true. The intersection is not the entire required mask, so all is false. Logical AND asks a different question: are both integer operands nonzero? They are, so logical and also prints true, even though one required permission bit is missing. These three lines show how an authorization check can be wrong without a compiler error. Name the desired predicate before writing an expression. If an operation needs both capabilities, test all required bits rather than merely finding one overlap.
actions: Predict all three booleans and explain why two true results still do not prove all bits exist.

question.prompt: Which expression should require both bits in required?
question.answer: (flags & required) == required, with the mask chosen to represent exactly the required capabilities.

slides.title: Replacement must remove old one-bits first
keyPoints: OR can turn bits on but cannot turn them off
Clear exactly the destination mask
Preserve every unselected position
slides.narration: The low two bits of old_word are both one, so the old field is three. We want the new field to be one. OR alone cannot clear the old second bit, leaving eleven as the complete decimal word. The corrected expression clears the low two positions, then inserts one, giving nine. The final comparison prints outside preserved=true because the high bit remains unchanged. This is not just a test of the requested new field. It checks the neighboring data too. A packed representation often holds several independent meanings in one word, so changing one field must not accidentally damage another field's state.
actions: Trace old field 3 changing to 1, then inspect the untouched high bit.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: Using old_value | (field << 4) leaves old one-bits in the field. It yields 0xB5, not 0x35.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Use word | (value << 4) without clearing. Setting 0xA5 to field 3 produces 0xB5.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Clear with word & ~mask, then insert with OR. Test clearing to zero, which immediately exposes a setter that can only add one-bits.

slides.title: Bits
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A bit is a binary digit with two possible values, conventionally zero and one.
A group of w bits has 2^w possible patterns.
Four bits have 16 patterns; eight bits have 256.
The number of patterns follows from independent choices: each new position doubles the number of combinations.
slides.narration: A bit is a binary digit with two possible values, conventionally zero and one. A group of w bits has 2^w possible patterns. Four bits have 16 patterns; eight bits have 256. The number of patterns follows from independent choices: each new position doubles the number of combinations. Physical devices need not store literal written zeros and ones. They distinguish states that are interpreted as those values. Software normally reasons above that physical level. What matters to the program is the behavior promised by the storage and instruction interfaces, including whether a read or write is atomic for the particular object and access. A bit pattern is an ordered collection of bits. If bits are numbered from the least significant position, bit i contributes a weight of 2^i to an unsigned interpretation. The pattern 10110110 therefore represents 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182 when treated as an unsigned eight-bit value. The pattern itself has not changed if another interpretation calls it a negative signed number. This distinction explains why a debugger can show the same storage in several formats. A display format is a lens on the stored representation. It does not alter the bytes or prove that the chosen interpretation matches the program’s intended type. Boolean operations combine truth values. AND is true when both inputs are true. OR is true when at least one is true. XOR is true when the inputs differ. NOT reverses a truth value. Applied independently to corresponding bit positions, these operations become bitwise operations on a word. Logical operators such as && and || are not substitutes for bitwise & and | . Logical operators convert operands to truth values and short-circuit evaluation. Bitwise operators operate on integral representations after the applicable promotions. x && y asks whether both are nonzero; x & y preserves positions where both patterns have a one.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Binary uses base two.
Each position has twice the weight of the position to its right.
Leading zeroes change the displayed width but not the unsigned value.
slides.narration: Binary uses base two. Each position has twice the weight of the position to its right. 110101 means 1 × 32 + 1 × 16 + 0 × 8 + 1 × 4 + 0 × 2 + 1 × 1 , giving 53. Leading zeroes change the displayed width but not the unsigned value. Binary notation makes masks and bit fields visible, but it becomes long for addresses and large integers. Use it when the positions themselves are the subject of the explanation. When only the value matters, decimal or hexadecimal may be easier to read. Decimal uses base ten. The number 347 means 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 7 . Decimal is convenient for human counts and measurements, but it does not reveal power-of-two boundaries as clearly as binary or hexadecimal. A numeral is a notation for a value, not a storage format. Writing 255 in source does not mean the executable stores the three character bytes '2' , '5' , and '5' . A numeric literal is translated as a value; a string literal is a sequence of character-code units. Distinguish these when designing parsers or examining file contents. Hexadecimal uses base sixteen, with digits 0 through 9 and A through F . One hexadecimal digit represents exactly four bits. Thus 0xB6 corresponds to 1011 0110 . Two hex digits describe an eight-bit byte without the visual length of eight binary digits. Hexadecimal is especially useful for alignment and field boundaries. An address ending in a hexadecimal zero is divisible by sixteen. Clearing the lowest hexadecimal digit rounds down to a sixteen-byte boundary. This visual rule works because sixteen is a power of two, not because hexadecimal has a special relationship with memory beyond its notation. To convert an unsigned binary or hexadecimal numeral to decimal, sum each digit multiplied by its positional weight. To convert a nonnegative decimal integer to another base, repeatedly divide by that base and collect remainders from last to first. For 182 in base sixteen, 182 = 11 × 16 + 6 , so the digits are B6 . For fractional values, positions to the right of the point use negative powers of the base. Binary 0.101 equals 1/2 + 0/4 + 1/8 = 0.625 . A finite decimal fraction need not have a finite binary expansion. That fact will explain many floating-point surprises in Chapter 5.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Bitwise AND, written & , retains a one only where both operands have one.
It is commonly used to test or extract fields.
If flags & mask is zero, none of the masked bits are set.
If the requirement is that all masked bits are set, test (flags & mask) == mask instead.
slides.narration: Bitwise AND, written & , retains a one only where both operands have one. It is commonly used to test or extract fields. If flags & mask is zero, none of the masked bits are set. If the requirement is that all masked bits are set, test (flags & mask) == mask instead. These two predicates are different. With mask 0b1100 and flags 0b0100 , “any” is true but “all” is false. A permission check that confuses them can authorize an operation based on only part of the required state. Name helper functions according to the exact predicate they implement. Bitwise OR, written | , sets a bit when either input has it set. flags |= mask turns on the selected bits while leaving other positions unchanged. It does not toggle them: applying the same OR operation twice has the same result as applying it once. This idempotence is useful for accumulating capabilities or marking completed phases. It is not automatically thread-safe. Two ordinary read-modify-write expressions on a shared word can race even when they set different bits. Use an atomic operation or a lock when multiple threads update the same shared object. Bitwise XOR, written ^ , sets a bit when the input bits differ. flags ^= mask toggles selected positions. XORing with the same mask twice restores the original pattern because each selected bit is flipped twice. XOR can also compare patterns: a ^ b marks their differing positions. It does not provide cryptographic security by itself. A repeated fixed XOR mask is a reversible encoding, not a secure encryption design. In systems code, use XOR for clearly defined bit manipulation rather than as an unexplained clever trick. Bitwise NOT, written ~ , flips every bit in the promoted operand type. That last phrase matters: applying ~ to a small integer type often first promotes it to int . The result may therefore have a wider type than the original byte. To clear selected bits in a word, use word &= ~mask with a mask of a suitable unsigned word type. When displaying or storing a smaller result, perform the intended conversion explicitly. Do not assume that a unary operator preserves the width of an eight-bit input merely because the variable was declared as a byte. A left shift moves bits toward more significant positions and fills low positions with zero. For unsigned values, it corresponds to multiplication by a power of two with reduction to the result type’s width. The shift count must be nonnegative and smaller than the width of the promoted left operand. Use unsigned types for field manipulation. The signed rules differ across language versions, and mathematical multiplication may overflow even when a target instruction happens to discard high bits. A shift by the full width is not a portable way to create zero. Handle full-width masks as an explicit special case. [ R36 ] For unsigned values, right shift fills high positions with zero and corresponds to division by a power of two with the fractional part discarded. It is the natural operation for moving a field down to bit zero before masking it. C17 leaves the right shift of a negative signed integer implementation-defined. C++20 specifies the signed result consistently with rounding division by a power of two toward negative infinity. This differs from signed integer / , which truncates toward zero. To avoid accidental dependence on these distinctions in binary formats, decode fields into unsigned values first. [ R8 , R36 ] A mask is a pattern that selects positions. A single-bit mask at position k can be formed as a correctly typed unsigned one shifted by k , after checking the count. A low- n -bit mask is often written (1u << n) - 1 , but that expression fails when n reaches the type width. Define the allowed field width and position before constructing a mask. For a 32-bit word, require width <= 32 , position <= 32 , and width <= 32 - position . The subtraction form avoids overflow in position + width . Handle width zero and width 32 deliberately. To extract a field of width w beginning at bit p , shift the word right by p , then AND with a low- w -bit mask. In notation, field = (word >> p) & mask . The result is right-justified and independent of unrelated high bits. For word = 0xB6 , p = 2 , and w = 3 , the shifted value is 0x2D ; masking with 0x07 yields 5. The selected bits are positions 4, 3, and 2, read as 101 . Write down the numbering convention before tracing; formats sometimes number bits in a different direction. Insertion has two separate operations: clear the destination field, then OR in the new field value. Merely ORing the new value leaves old one-bits in place. The usual expression is (word & ~shifted_mask) | ((value & mask) << position) for a validated nonempty field. Masking the incoming value truncates it. That may be the intended policy, but protocol encoders often should reject a value that does not fit instead. Silent truncation can hide invalid input. Decide whether the operation is a bit-level replacement or a validated semantic assignment, then make that decision visible in its interface.

slides.title: Width rules apply after integer promotion
keyPoints: Small integer operands can promote
The shift count must fit the promoted width
Use an unsigned word type deliberately
slides.narration: A variable described as a byte does not guarantee that every expression involving it stays byte-wide. Small integer operands can be promoted before a bitwise operation. In particular, complement may produce a wider result than the original object suggests. Shifts also have requirements: the count must be nonnegative and less than the width of the promoted left operand. Shifting by the full width is not a portable shortcut for zero. A reusable field helper should state its word type, allowed positions, and allowed widths, then handle special cases explicitly. These rules matter during source-level reasoning even if one machine instruction happens to mask its shift count.

slides.title: Idempotent setting is different from toggling
keyPoints: OR with a mask sets selected bits
Repeating the same OR changes nothing further
XOR twice restores the previous pattern
slides.narration: An operation is idempotent when repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. Setting a ready flag with OR has that property: once the bit is one, another identical OR leaves it one. XOR does something different. It toggles selected bits, so repeating the same toggle returns them to their previous values. This difference matters when a message might be retried. A repeated set-ready operation can preserve the intended state, while a repeated toggle-ready operation can undo it. keyPoints: A byte address names a position
Typed pointer steps count elements
Representation inspection is not permission to access anywhere
slides.narration: On the reference platform, increasing a byte address by one moves one eight-bit byte. Increasing an int pointer by one moves one int element, typically several bytes on that platform. The arithmetic units differ. More importantly, neither view grants access beyond the live object or range. A page can be mapped while a particular array index is still invalid. Character and byte access can inspect object representations under the language rules, but raw representation is not automatically a stable file format. slides.title: Decide whether an oversized field is rejected or truncated
keyPoints: Masking can silently discard high bits
A checked setter can reject a value that does not fit
The policy belongs in the interface
slides.narration: A three-bit field can represent values from zero through seven. If a setter receives nine and masks it with seven, the inserted field becomes one. slides.narration: A good packed-field test has more than one assertion. Extract the field after a successful update and compare it with the requested value. Then remove the field positions from both old and new words and compare the rest. Those checks cover the intended change and the protected neighbors. For rejected positions, widths, or values, confirm that the original word remains unchanged if that is the setter's contract. A helper that returns failure after partially clearing bits creates a much harder recovery problem. Exhaustive testing is practical for small modeled words and can uncover mistakes that a few visually convenient hexadecimal examples miss.

slides.narration: Before memorizing a mask expression, practice explaining it in words. We clear these positions because the old field may contain ones that the new value does not need. We insert this checked value after shifting it to the declared starting position. We leave these other positions untouched because they belong to other fields. That explanation is easier to review than a clever expression with unexplained constants. Named masks, checked helper boundaries, and small tests let a format grow without scattering assumptions through many callers. example.title: Replace only one packed field
example.text:
const unsigned mask = 0xFu << 4;
    const unsigned result = (old_value & ~mask) | (field << 4);
explain: 0xF is hexadecimal 15: four one-bits. The u suffix selects an unsigned type. << 4 shifts that group four positions to select bits 4 through 7.
~ flips the mask bits. & clears the selected old field; << positions the new field; | combines the non-overlapping groups. The old A field becomes 3 while the low 5 remains.
example.invariant: Only bits 4–7 change. The new field fits in four bits before it is shifted into place.
